concepts.title: The Date on the Bag
concepts.hook: Find the roast date on this bag. Go. (Person holds up a grocery-store coffee bag, turning it over and over, searching.)
concepts.insight: I buy 'fresh' coffee at the store and have no idea when it was actually roasted.
concepts.summary: One person in a kitchen hunts for a roast date on a generic bag and can't find one. They sigh, then pick up a Brasswick bag and point straight to the printed roast date. Voiceover or on-camera line: 'Whole beans, roast date on every bag. That's it. That's the flex.' Close on them grinding a few beans, with a text overlay: 'Brasswick small-batch roasted coffee. Monthly box.' The story is a brand that simply tells you when it roasted.
concepts.note: The 'find the date' challenge is a strong scroll-stopper and puts the roast-date proof point front and center. It's held back by a text overlay and a label-reading close-up, both risky for AI video, and the 'that's the flex' line is a bit cute. The subscription is only a tag at the end.

concepts.title: Second-Week Slump
concepts.hook: Day 1: wow. Day 12: ...is it me? (Person sniffs a mug and frowns on a handwritten calendar overlay.)
concepts.insight: My coffee tastes flat by the second week and I don't know if it's me or the beans.
concepts.summary: A single person at a counter does a quick 'day 1 vs day 12' mime of tasting their old coffee, getting more deflated. They then check the roast date on a Brasswick bag and grind whole beans right before brewing. Line: 'Now I know how old it is, and I grind it when I'm ready.' Ends with the monthly box arriving at the door, so a new bag shows up on a regular rhythm. Only claims: whole beans, roast date printed, monthly subscription.
concepts.note: The 'is it me or the beans?' insight is relatable and fresh, and it ties roast date and grinding to the subscription rhythm. A handwritten calendar overlay and the day 1 vs day 12 mime depend on text and acting, which AI models handle poorly, and the many beats crowd 20 seconds.

concepts.title: One Place, Not a Mystery
concepts.hook: Where is your coffee from? Not the country. The actual place. (Person points at a vague 'premium blend' label with a raised eyebrow.)
concepts.insight: Every bag has a vague 'premium blend' label. I can't tell where it's from or who grew it.
concepts.summary: Two friends in a kitchen: one reads the vague 'premium blend' label aloud and shrugs. The other slides over a Brasswick bag and says, 'Single-origin. One place, not a mystery blend.' They pour a cup together and the first friend smells it and nods. Warm brand-story tone about knowing what's in your cup, with a closing line: 'Small-batch roasted, single-origin, Brasswick.' No invented farm details, just the origin promise.
concepts.note: The origin question is a decent hook and speaks to people who care where coffee comes from. But it needs two people, readable label text and dialogue, and it is a familiar 'vague blend vs ours' comparison. It never mentions the subscription, so it does little for the first-box goal.

concepts.title: The Ritual Minute
concepts.hook: (Close-up: a hand pours whole beans into a grinder, sound turned up.) This is the best 30 seconds of my day.
concepts.insight: I want my morning brew to feel like a small ritual I look forward to, not just caffeine.
concepts.summary: A quiet, sound-led morning scene in one kitchen: beans rattle into the grinder, the grind, the pour, the first sip. Soft voiceover: 'Whole beans, roasted in small batches. I grind, I brew, I stand here for a minute.' Shows that a basic setup is enough: one simple brewer on the counter, no fuss. End card: 'Brasswick. Your morning, slowed down by a minute.'
concepts.note: A sound-led close-up of beans and a grinder is easy to produce and feels good in feed. But coffee ritual is the most overused angle in the category, the hook is soft, and nothing here gives a reason to subscribe or to pick Brasswick. Fine mood piece, weak ad.

concepts.title: Stop Thinking About Coffee
concepts.hook: I haven't run out of coffee in months. (Person casually opens the door to a Brasswick box on the step.)
concepts.insight: I want good coffee to just show up so I stop thinking about it, and I'm tired of grabbing whatever is left on the shelf.
concepts.summary: A person brings in the monthly box, opens it, and checks the roast date on the new bag. Addresses the fear of piling up with a light line: 'A new bag on a regular rhythm, and the roast date tells me where I am.' Quick cuts: old bag nearly empty, new bag arriving, a fresh grind. Close: 'Brasswick small-batch roasted coffee, monthly box. Start your first one.' Aimed at driving the first subscription.
concepts.note: It is the most direct route to a first subscription, with a clear CTA and a roast-date tie-in. The hook is a flat claim and 'a box shows up at the door' is a stock subscription story. It is simple to shoot, but it feels like an ad and not a real person.

reason: The 'find the date' challenge is a strong scroll-stopper and puts the roast-date proof point front and center. It's held back by a text overlay and a label-reading close-up, both risky for AI video, and the 'that's the flex' line is a bit cute. The subscription is only a tag at the end.
